title: Governance in risk & issue management
blurb: Explain why governance matters for risks and issues: appetite and tolerances, ownership, escalation routes, reporting and control of contingency.
question: A new project manager discovers that her predecessor kept no risk register, spent contingency without approval and told the board nothing until the project was £400,000 over budget. The sponsor asks her to explain why governance of risks and issues matters. What should she say?

teach.h: Who decides, and on what basis
teach.body: Governance is the framework of authority, accountability and control within which a project is run: policies, processes, roles and delegated responsibilities with their tolerances. Applied to risks and issues, it answers six questions. How much risk will we take? Who owns each risk? Who may decide what? When must something be escalated? How does the board find out? Who controls the contingency? In plain English: the rules that make sure the right people take the right risk decisions at the right time.

teach.h: Why governance matters for risks and issues
head: Governance sets…
So that…
rows: Responses are consistent and limits are clear
Every risk and issue has someone accountable
Decisions are taken at the right level
The sponsor and board see real exposure early
Reserves are spent only on approved needs
Policy and regulation are met; projects compare
teach.caption: These rules are usually written into the risk management plan within the project management plan.

teach.body: RISK APPETITE is the amount and type of risk an organisation is willing to take in pursuit of its objectives. It is set at the top and reflects strategy: a hospital has a very low appetite for patient-safety risk; a tech start-up may have a high appetite for market risk. TOLERANCES are the permitted deviations delegated to each level, such as ±£20,000 or ±2 weeks for the PM. Inside tolerance, that level acts; beyond it, it escalates.

teach.h: Delegated authority for risks and issues
teach.caption: Each level decides within its tolerance and escalates what lies beyond it. Management reserve sits with the sponsor or board.

teach.h: Risk owner vs risk action owner
teach.caption: Separating oversight from execution keeps accountability clear. The risk owner confirms when a risk can be closed.

teach.body: With no register, nobody could see the exposure. With contingency spent informally, nothing was left when the ground risk actually hit. With no reporting, the board learned late, when the options had gone and confidence collapsed. Good governance would have meant an agreed appetite, named risk owners, monthly risk reports to the board, approved drawdowns, prompt escalation at the tolerance line and an independent assurance review checking that the process was really being followed.

teach.h: Governing risk in linear and iterative projects

rows.label: Tolerances
values: Set per stage on time and cost
Time and cost fixed; scope flexes

teach.text: Traps: (1) Appetite is NOT tolerance: appetite is how much risk the organisation will take overall; a tolerance is the deviation limit delegated to one role. (2) Governance doesn't mean sending everything to the board: it makes sure each decision sits at the RIGHT level. (3) The sponsor doesn't run the risk register; the PM manages it and risk owners own individual risks.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: It sets risk appetite and tolerances, so responses are consistent and limits are clear.
It defines ownership and roles, so every risk and issue has someone accountable.
It sets escalation routes, so decisions are made at the right level and in time.
It ensures transparent reporting to the sponsor and board, so there are no surprises.
It controls contingency and ensures compliance, protecting the business case.
Governance: authority, accountability and control for risk and issue decisions.
Appetite (organisation-wide) differs from tolerance (a delegated limit per role).
Risk owner is accountable; risk action owner carries out the response.
Escalate beyond tolerance: PM, then sponsor, then board or portfolio.
Contingency drawdown is approved, recorded and reported, never spent informally.

summary: You can now explain why governance matters in risk and issue management: it sets appetite and tolerances, assigns ownership, defines escalation, keeps the board informed and controls contingency. You can also show how this works in linear and iterative projects and what goes wrong without it.

A.q: What is meant by an organisation's RISK APPETITE?
options: The deviation a PM may absorb before escalating
The money set aside to deal with known risks
The amount of risk it is willing to take on
The list of risks the team has identified
A.why: Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk an organisation is willing to take in pursuit of its objectives.

whyNot.0: The deviation a PM may absorb is their tolerance, a delegated limit.
whyNot.1: Money set aside for known risks is contingency.
whyNot.3: The list of identified risks is the risk register.

A.q: A PM's time tolerance is ±2 weeks. A risk has occurred and will delay handover by five weeks. What does good governance require?
options: Escalate to the sponsor, as tolerance is breached
Absorb the delay quietly and try to recover it later
Ask the team to vote on whether to tell anyone
Reset the tolerance to six weeks and carry on
A.why: The delay exceeds the PM's delegated tolerance, so the decision must be escalated to the sponsor, who has the authority to make it.

whyNot.1: Hiding a breach of tolerance takes the decision away from the person entitled to make it.
whyNot.2: Escalation isn't optional or a matter for a vote; the tolerance defines it.
whyNot.3: A PM can't change their own tolerances; they are set by the level above.

A.q: Who is normally accountable for making sure a particular risk is monitored and managed?
options: The risk action owner
The project board
The end users
The risk owner
A.why: The risk owner is accountable for a specific risk: monitoring it and making sure suitable responses are in place.

whyNot.0: The risk action owner carries out a particular response action, not overall accountability for the risk.
whyNot.1: The board sets direction and takes escalated decisions; it doesn't own individual risks.
whyNot.2: Users may be affected by risks, but they aren't normally accountable for managing them.

B.q: What is the main reason drawdown of contingency is controlled through governance?
options: So the PM never needs to report on any risks again
So it is spent only on approved, real risk events
So suppliers can use it without asking first
So the business case never needs to be revised
B.why: Governance makes sure contingency is used only for the risks it was set aside for, with approval at the right level, and that what remains is visible.

whyNot.0: Drawdown is itself reported; governance increases reporting, not removes it.
whyNot.2: Suppliers have no right to draw on the client's contingency.
whyNot.3: Heavy drawdown may well trigger a review of the business case.

B.q: Each month, a board receives a report showing the top ten risks, their trends and the contingency remaining. Which governance purpose does this mainly serve?
options: Identifying new risks
Transferring risk to others
Realising the benefits
Oversight and transparency
B.why: Regular reporting gives the board visibility of real exposure, so it can oversee the project and step in early.

whyNot.0: Identification is done by the project team; the report communicates risks already identified.
whyNot.1: Reporting to the board doesn't move financial impact to a third party.
whyNot.2: Benefits realisation is about achieving benefits after handover, not risk reporting.

B.q: Which TWO of these are set or controlled by governance in risk management? 1 Risk appetite and tolerances. 2 The actual probability of each threat. 3 Escalation routes and risk ownership. 4 Whether a supplier's factory floods.
options: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Governance sets the rules: how much risk to take, the limits at each level, who owns what and how things are escalated.

whyNot.1: Governance sets appetite, but it can't set the real probability of a threat; analysis estimates it.
whyNot.2: Neither the probability of a threat nor a flood is controlled by governance.
whyNot.3: Governance defines escalation and ownership, but it can't control whether a flood happens.

C.q: On an agile programme, the product owner swaps two backlog features to deal with a risk, staying within the release's fixed time and cost. Later, a different risk threatens to push back the release date. How should governance treat the two?
options: Both are product owner decisions within the team
First within delegated authority; second escalated
Both must go to the board through change control
First needs the sponsor; second is the team's call
C.why: Reprioritising scope within fixed time and cost is delegated to the product owner. Threatening the fixed release date breaches tolerance, so it goes to the sponsor.

whyNot.0: The release date is a fixed limit; threatening it is beyond the product owner's authority.
whyNot.2: Sending a within-tolerance backlog swap to the board puts the decision at the wrong level.
whyNot.3: This reverses the levels: the swap is within authority, the date threat is not.

C.q: A PM keeps an excellent risk register but never shares it beyond the team. The sponsor is shocked when a major risk occurs. Which governance purpose has failed?
options: Identifying risks early in the life cycle
Analysing the probability and impact of each risk
Transparent reporting to the sponsor and board
Choosing proactive responses to each threat
C.why: The risks were identified and analysed, but governance also needs exposure reported upwards so the sponsor and board are never surprised.

whyNot.0: The register was excellent, so identification worked.
whyNot.1: Analysis was done; the failure was in sharing it.
whyNot.3: Responses may have been sound; the problem was that decision makers weren't told.

C.q: Which statement about risk appetite and tolerance is correct?
options: Appetite is set by the PM; tolerance by the team
They mean the same and can be used interchangeably
Tolerance applies only to opportunities, not threats
Appetite is overall; tolerance is a delegated limit
C.why: Appetite is how much risk the organisation will take overall; tolerances are the deviation limits delegated to each role, which trigger escalation.

whyNot.0: Appetite is set at the top of the organisation, and tolerances are delegated downwards from above.
whyNot.1: They are related but different: one is organisation-wide, the other a limit for a role.
whyNot.2: Tolerances apply to deviations in time, cost and other measures, whatever caused them.

reteach.title: Think of running a music festival
reteach.question: A festival has a director, a security chief, stage managers and a weather fund. How do they decide who handles which risk?

blocks.body: The festival's owners have zero appetite for crowd-safety risk, but are happy to gamble on unknown bands. The security chief owns the crowd-crush risk; stewards carry out the actions (barriers, one-way routes). Stage managers may spend up to £2,000 fixing problems on the day; anything bigger goes to the director. The weather fund is held by the director and only released with her say-so. And the owners get a risk briefing every week in the run-up.

blocks.text: The owners don't fix a broken microphone, and a stage manager doesn't cancel the festival. Governance is about each decision sitting at the right level.

explain.body: Appetite tells everyone how bold or cautious to be, so responses are consistent with strategy. Tolerances tell each role how far things may drift before they must escalate, so problems surface at the right time.

test.q: A hospital board states a very low appetite for risks to patient safety. What should this mean for a ward-relocation project?
options: Patient-safety risks can be accepted to save money
Patient-safety threats get strong, early responses
The PM need not record any patient-safety risks
Only opportunities need managing on the project
test.why: A low appetite means little exposure is tolerated, so patient-safety threats should be avoided or reduced firmly and early.

whyNot.0: Accepting them to save money contradicts a low appetite.
whyNot.2: Low appetite calls for more visibility of these risks, not less.
whyNot.3: Threats must still be managed; low appetite makes that more important.

explain.body: Governance names a risk owner for each risk (accountable, chosen for their authority) and risk action owners for each response (they do the work). It also names the issue owner. Clear ownership means nothing falls between the cracks.

head: Role
For a risk, they…
rows: Run the process and the register

test.q: An engineer is installing flood barriers as the agreed response to a site-flooding risk owned by the site director. What is the engineer's role?
options: Risk owner
Project sponsor
Risk action owner
Assurance reviewer
test.why: The engineer is carrying out a specific response action, so they are the risk action owner. The site director remains the risk owner.

whyNot.0: The site director is the risk owner, accountable for the risk overall.
whyNot.1: The sponsor owns the business case and takes escalated decisions.
whyNot.3: Assurance reviewers independently check the project; they don't implement responses.

explain.body: Escalation routes make sure decisions beyond one level's authority reach someone who can make them, quickly. Regular, honest reporting of risks, issues and contingency to the sponsor and board means no surprises and decisions taken while options remain.

test.q: Why does governance require issues beyond tolerance to be escalated rather than handled by the PM?
options: The decision needs authority the PM does not hold
The PM is not allowed to analyse any issues at all
Escalation removes the PM's need to keep a log
Sponsors prefer to manage issues day to day
test.why: Beyond tolerance, the decision (more money, more time, less scope) belongs to someone with greater delegated authority.

whyNot.1: The PM analyses issues and brings options; they just can't decide those beyond tolerance.
whyNot.2: The PM still keeps the issue log and tracks the actions.
whyNot.3: Sponsors take escalated decisions; day-to-day management stays with the PM.

explain.body: Governance controls who may release contingency and management reserve, and makes sure every drawdown is recorded. A consistent, organisation-wide process lets risks be compared and rolled up across projects, lets assurance check it is followed, and meets policy and regulation.

test.q: Which is NOT a benefit of a consistent, organisation-wide risk management process?
options: Risks can be compared and rolled up across projects
Assurance can check that the process is followed
Every risk is guaranteed to be eliminated
Policy and regulatory requirements are met
test.why: No process eliminates every risk. Consistency improves comparison, assurance and compliance, not certainty.

whyNot.0: A common approach lets risks be compared and aggregated across the portfolio.
whyNot.1: A defined process gives assurance reviewers something to check against.
whyNot.3: A consistent process helps the organisation meet its policies and regulations.
